title: 7 Factors 1 Intro
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces a series on the Seven Factors of Awakening, taught in the weeks before Rohatsu, and begins with mindfulness as the center of the list. Nomon sets the factors beside the 52 mental factors of the Abhidharma, then reads them as both a stepwise progression and a balance with mindfulness as the fulcrum. Bhikkhu Bodhi's reading of the Satipatthana Sutta's praise of mindfulness as that which leads forward without turning back leads into the four frames of reference: body, sensations and reactions, thinking and emotion, and lists such as the five hindrances. The week's practice is to notice which hindrance is most present and feel the body in that moment.

sentences.text: So tonight, in these weeks leading up to our celebration of Buddha's enlightenment, which is like the high holy days of Zen, the Rohatsu celebration coming up in December, I thought we would have a series of talks and take up one of the Buddha's teachings called the Seven Factors of Awakening, or the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
Buddha identified seven aspects of mind, or factors of mind, that he said were particularly important to cultivate and recognize and uncover, if you will, to support awakening.
A really important subtext of all these teachings, which we have to remind ourselves of again and again, is that the mind matters.
And not just the contents, or the story, or the topic of the thinking, but the full dimensions of the mind.
The way the mind flows, the ways the currents of the mind get caught on things, get constricted in various ways, and then can open up again and be unlimbered and freed again.

The mind matters in that it helps for us to have a better understanding of our relationship to the different aspects of mind, our relationship to our thinking and our emotions, our relationship to perception.
It all matters.
It's all somewhat habitual, though.
So these practices and teachings remind us that the mind matters and that it can be practiced with and investigated in various ways.
Maybe we have more of an opportunity in life to recognize the patterning and the function of mind and practice with that in a way that is conducive to awakening.
It's interesting, because we know full well that the body has to be cared for: that what we eat matters, that getting enough exercise matters, that getting enough sleep matters.
We don't always take the most skillful action that we could with the body.
We miss a day or a month of exercise.
We stay up too late and so on.
But we're not surprised when we're tired the next day.
We know that that's how it goes.
We know that we have some obligation to care for the body if we want to be happy and healthy.

But somehow we have the idea that the mind should just take care of itself, and that if the external circumstances are right, the mind will just be fine, whatever we think the external circumstances are.
Maybe having the right job or having good friends who treat us the way they're supposed to, according to us.
Or maybe we think the right spiritual practice will give us the right external circumstances and the mind will just be fine: happy, settled, relaxed mind.
And it's not that we totally ignore the mind.
We really value learning.
We really value learning in our culture, and education.
But in that education we privilege content.
We value people who become experts in the content areas of knowledge.
And we do experience learning, I think, as satisfying in itself.

We expect the learning of stuff to lead to some happiness and some contentment, either directly or maybe because learning the right stuff will lead to better external circumstances, which will then make us happy, right?
Like a good career or something like this.
So these teachings of the Buddha that I want to bring up, these seven factors, are more about the process of mind and less about the content of mind.
More about how the mind works.
What are the aspects and qualities of mind, what the Buddha called factors.
I forgot to look up what word is being translated as factors, but I think it's a fairly literal translation.
I don't know if it was the Buddha or a little bit later, the great meditative scientists who created the Abhidharma, the system of Buddhist psychology.
I think that's mostly after the Buddha's life.
But they decided that there are exactly 52 mental factors, 52 aspects of mind, which you can think of as a deck, like a deck of cards.
We all hopefully start with a full deck.
Not all of us have a full deck, right?
So that's a problem.
Then you have psychology and so on.
You need to add some cards in there.
Or maybe we have a few jokers where we should have had a seven of clubs.
We have a joker standing in and then it turns into something else.
What's interesting too about this is just the tremendous access that we now have to this amount of scholarship that's happened in English, and how accessible things are on the internet.
I'm not going to go into it, but I had heard of these different factors, different dharmas of mind.
And I always wondered, well, they always highlight a few, but what's the whole list?
I could never find out the whole list.
You had to be a major Abhidharma scholar and go to some dusty book in a deep university library to find this out.
At least that used to be true.
Now, Google: 52 mental factors.
And I got a very nicely organized PDF, very clear, nice diagrams.
So I won't tell you what they all are, but some are positive things.
Some are not so positive.
Some are things that are always present.
They're organized in different groups.
Some are things that are always present or very common, like perception is a mental factor.
And other ones are things that come and go.
Some things are associated with greed and hatred.
Some things are associated with kindness and generosity and so on.
So they've got this way of organizing the mental factors.
There's one group that's called the 25 beautiful mental factors.
These are positive things that we think of.
Tranquility is one, for instance.
And there are different versions and permutations.
So anyway, there are all these mental factors.
Our psychology is a psychology from the outside looking in, to a certain extent.
Our sciences in general are the outside looking in.
Buddhist psychology was an experiential psychology of experience from the inside out.
They carefully watched their thoughts and figured out they could organize them into 52 categories.
And the Buddha picked out seven of these that he felt were most important to this process of waking up.
So what do we mean by waking up?
An important question.
It might be waking up to a flexible, interpenetrated, open-hearted life where we don't cling on to our problems as problems in the same way that we might do before these factors are fully enlivened.
Where there's just the joy of being in experience, including everything, including tears and troubles, triumphs and joys, things arising, things passing away.
So the Buddha's awakening is being awake to, or present to, or free in the middle of everything that's coming and going.
It also implies a lack of quite a few unhealthy things that we do.
Usually in traditional Buddhism these things are described in the negative, so we have to make it up in English in the postmodern era if we want to say it in a positive way.
But in traditional Buddhism it's always described in the negative, like awakening is characterized by a lack of greed, a lack of hatred, a lack of confusion and delusion.
By having experiences that we don't add suffering to, that we don't add confusion to.
In the positive, maybe something like just showing up, really showing up for the full show of our life.
That's my definition, I wrote in here my definition of the moment, but I wrote this a few hours ago, so it's already changed.
But showing up, really showing up for our life and not being hindered by our life.
And so there's some natural joy there when suffering is gone.
I think we think about things in terms of states.
We would like to have a happier state.
So it's possible to think of awakening as a state, a state where you're really just right there.

Or maybe it's more helpful to think of this as a process: showing up more fully, more often, more of the time, less often being caught in confusion, delusion, anger, wishing things were other than the way they are.
I remember we used to always pass around Joko Beck, and remember those days, used to pass around Joko Beck, and she talks in terms of percentages in there, actually.
She's like, it would be really nice if you could be, like, 13% of the time not reacting instead of, whichever way she said it.
Her percentages, I forget what she said exactly, but just a few percentage more and you make the happier choice.
That would be great.
So here are the seven mental factors that lead to awakening, says the Buddha.
I'll read them to you and we'll talk about them a little bit in aggregate, and I have a handout for you too for later.
They are mindfulness, discernment, diligence, joy, lightness and ease (that's one), samadhi or concentration, and wisdom.
So: mindfulness, discernment or inquiry, diligence, joy, lightness and ease, which can also be tranquility or calm, concentrated awareness, and wisdom.
What's interesting is there are two primary ways that this list is looked at and commented on.
One is as a stepwise list, which is probably about the first thing we think of.
That first you practice mindfulness, become a little more aware of what's actually happening as opposed to what you think might be happening.
That mindfulness leads you to more accurately discern what's happening, and so then discernment can be there.
You can inquire more accurately, and you can be more interested too, actually, in the actual moments of unfolding experience at a very baseline experiential level.
So mindfulness leads to discernment.
And then once you're starting to be more mindful of what's happening and discerning more accurately what's happening, diligence arises naturally.
Like, wow, this is really helping me.
I feel grounded, I feel aware, this feels like less of my crazy story.
So you really get motivated.
I'm just like, yes, this is great.
Then once you're motivated and discerning and mindful, actually joy arises, and you've probably all experienced this at different times.
You suddenly feel like, wow, I actually feel really happy.
It's not because I got some [unclear: "benny"] from somebody.
It's just the happiness of being alive arises.
And the joy, piti I think is the word in Pali, is a kind of exuberant, effervescent joy.
Then once that's arising, the next one is more of a calm, tranquility type of joy, which is translated, my current favorite being, lightness and ease.
So easefulness.
So you see there's a progression here.
Once there's a lightfulness and an ease and a joy, then naturally we're pretty concentrated, right?
We're just right here.
We don't need to be distracting ourselves anymore, and we're less distracted by the things that are running around us.
And all that leads to wisdom.
Wisdom here means discernment into what is going to keep this whole thing running in a positive way.
What's skillful here?
What's unskillful?
What's going to lead to more joy and less suffering in myself and others?
So that's how we would naturally think of it: I do this, then I get this, then I get this.
But another way to look at it is that we actually already have all these things.
All these qualities are qualities of mind that are always present.
But we don't always notice them.
They're somehow occluded or covered up or jumbled.
Another way to look at this list of seven is that it's a balancing.
If one thing is too big, then we let that calm down.
And we see if we can discern and notice and cultivate the things that we're not noticing in this list of seven.
That's maybe helpful to us too.
Because when you think of it as a progression, you're like, I've got a program here.
Time to get busy.
And time to fail.
And time to fail.
The minute we have a program and we're trying to get busy and accomplish something, we're set up for failure.
So this balance idea can help us.
There's a balance between approaches, and one of the approaches is balance.
In the balance idea, mindfulness is like the fulcrum in the middle.
On one side are the first three, which are active.
The next three, I mean, discernment, diligence and joy are on one side of the balance scale.
You're discerning, you're diligent, you're exuberant, you're excited, this is working.
It's uplifted on one side.
And the other side is more of a cooling out on the other side of the balance scale: calming down, being concentrated, accessing wisdom.
But mindfulness is right in the center.
So I just want to talk a little bit about mindfulness tonight, and we'll talk a little bit about mindfulness next week too, because mindfulness is just so key.
And no wonder mindfulness hops the religion wall out into secular society.
I've been enjoying getting to participate in that myself.
This morning I actually had a class with 15 people, most of whom are very little interested in Buddhism but are interested in mindfulness and are interested in happiness.

In the main sutra that we have about mindfulness, which is called the Satipatthana Sutta, in the old teachings of Buddha, which just means the sutra on mindfulness, the Buddha is really enthusiastic about mindfulness.
He uses a fairly unusual adjective.
I forget what the adjective was in Pali right now, but it's been difficult to translate, apparently.
Originally it was translated as wonderful, or the best of all, or just superior.
He says mindfulness is the superior, best of all thing.

But then the other day I was reading Bhikkhu Bodhi, one of these amazing educated Westerners who were ordained in Sri Lanka and just devoted his life to studying this early Buddhist material and translating it.
He was a New York lawyer originally, I think.
So he was a very reliable translator.
I was reading some commentary by him on this word, which I'll bring you next week.
He said well, actually it doesn't exactly mean the best or superior.
It means that which only leads forward without regression, without turning back.
So that's what Bhikkhu Bodhi thinks this word is that the Buddha uses in the sutra to describe the process and the value of mindfulness: if you practice mindfulness, there's no going back.
It just leads forward to more awareness, more awakening, all these desirable qualities.
So that's nice.
You're not going to regress.
There's no regression.
You may regress from where you think you are, but that's a different problem.
That's what you think.
In that sutra he talks about four frames or four areas for practicing mindfulness.
I know we've talked about this many times, but it's worth bringing back to mind and really trying to memorize and remember it.
Sometimes these four areas are called foundations, like places you could really build something strong.
And just recently we were saying the other day that I've seen it retranslated as frames of reference for practice.
Frames of reference is nice because we always have a frame of reference.
We always have some view or some idea of who we are and what's happening, and we know that our frame of reference is somewhat limited.
So the Buddha is saying we'll take up a whole different frame of reference for a time in your practice.
Be mindful, meaning return to, be aware of, moment by moment, what's occurring within that frame, and let the other things be secondary.
And of course our main frame of reference is me, right?
Me, me, me, me.
So this is trying to bring up an alternative, which is pretty skillful.
I think we can't repress the me, me, me thing, right?
That doesn't work.
Sometimes you see people trying to strangle their me-ness, but it doesn't work.
We can bring forward an alternative and let the me, me, me be a little quieter.
So the four frames of reference: the first one is the body.
We practice actually feeling the sensations in the body.
We can move the body and take care of the body in different ways.

Yoga and exercise are part of this, but with an important qualifier: to do yoga, to do exercise, not as a way to fix the body or make the body stronger or solve some sort of problem of having a body, but to cultivate awareness of the body and feeling of the body, to really be inside the body.
In the sutra, the Buddha always uses a phrase, something like mindful of the body in the body, or the body as the body.
So watch out for our tendency to objectify everything, like making the body some object down there that the little mind control center is trying to take care of.
Beep, beep, body down there, body down there.
No, body from the inside out.
And in the foundation of mindfulness, the body includes the breath.
That's where breath awareness is.
That's part of why breath awareness is so central.
It's the first part of what he says is this one way of practicing.
So you feel the breathing body.
Again, we can also turn the breath into a mental object or an idea, so be sure when we're practicing that we're engaging the experience of breathing in the body.
That's the most important one.
Then the next three are all different aspects of what we think of as mind.
The second foundation, the first of those next three, is what's usually translated as feelings, which I find very problematic.
Sometimes they translate it as feeling tone.
But it really means, at a low level, what do we sense and how do we react to what we sense?
Really quickly, even before we think about it, just that gut level: I like this, I don't like this.
So lately I'm calling it sensations and reactions, before thinking.
It's being sensitive to how we lean in and out of experience all day: I don't like that, I don't like that, or neutral, which we usually don't notice.
Then the third one is the thinking itself, the way we use the mind to form things, to create things.
Sometimes they say mental formations, but from our frame it's thinking and emotion.

The practice is to be able to see thinking and emotion not, again, as the me, me, me getting what it wants or not getting what it wants and being very frustrated, but to see thoughts and emotions as events arising in the mind.
Oh, look, there's a thought.
And there it goes again.
And we get hooked up to these thoughts, and of course we notice some of them are quite a bit more charged than others, right?
But we just start to practice with it and actually feel the huge difference between something like "God, I hate it when she does that" and "Oh, a judgment's arising."
It's the same mental experience, but described in a different way: one very tight and clingy, and one liberating and fluid, allowing the judgment to come and to go.
What's interesting about the fourth of these four foundations of mindfulness, which are applied by this first of the seven factors, is that this gets confusing, so listen to this carefully.
We have the seven factors, and the first one is mindfulness.
When mindfulness is described, it's in these four categories, these four foundations.
The fourth one is basically a bunch of Buddhist lists that describe the patterning of reality.
And among the lists that are described is the seven factors of enlightenment.
So it all folds back in on itself in different ways that are a little frustrating to our Western mind, where we want a tree diagram: what's the first thing, what's the last thing.
One thing refers to another thing, and the other thing refers right back to the first thing.
So it's circular, but that's how the mind really works, it seems.
One of the lists in this fourth foundation is right back to the seven, but another one that's really important is the five hindrances.
The five hindrances are included in this final area of being mindful.
The way I've come to translate this final area, in the traditional translation, is mindfulness of dharmas, of experience.

I realize it's actually a list of habits and patterns from a certain frame.

So the five hindrances are also worth studying, and I'll give you a little handout when we get to the lobby with the five hindrances and these seven factors of enlightenment, because they're seen as working together in a certain way.
The seven factors are an antidote to the five hindrances.
And when the hindrances arrive, they're like signals.
They're like somebody waving a flag: time to study the seven factors, because the hindrances are arriving.
The five hindrances, I always had trouble remembering what they were, but then I realized it's actually pretty easy to remember.
There are two pairs of related qualities, the first four, and then the fifth one is doubt.
Doubt, right?
Doubting that any of this could ever work, doubting that we're ever going to change, big doubt.
The two pairs: desire and aversion are the first pair.
We want stuff, we don't want stuff.
Desire and aversion, which shows up all through Buddhism, right?
The second pair are dullness and restlessness: being a little too dull or too sleepy on the one hand, or a little too amped up or jaggy on the other hand.
These are not the usual English translations, but I'm on a real translation kick, so I think these are better.
Dullness is usually translated as sloth and torpor, which is so cute, but it's so dorky that you just chuckle and then you forget it.
Dullness I think we can relate to.
We often feel kind of dull, right?
Low energy, kind of down, not quite engaging with the world.
And sometimes we just sink into that dullness like oozy goop.
When these things arise, they're a way of encouraging us, which is interesting.
The way they look at these in Buddhism is purely as problems: don't want that, hindrance is bad, bad, bad, bad.
But the way it's looked at in the system is, well, actually when the hindrances arise, it's an encouragement to practice.
You're like, oh wow, I feel dull.
How do I work with that?
How do I bring forward the positive factors of awakening to work with that?
So I thought our task for this next week, if you want to, is to get a little familiar with these two lists.
Take the handout with you, read them, put them on the fridge or whatever.
But then especially see if you can notice what are the hindrances that are most present for me.
What are the hindrances that are arising most?
And can I practice mindfulness in that moment?
Can I feel the body when dullness arises, or whatever it is for you?
When agitation arises, can I feel the body?
Can I be mindful of the way I'm reacting to experience?
Can I be mindful of the thinking?
Then over the next however many weeks we'll just take each factor and maybe each hindrance, we'll see how long we'll spend on this, and come up with other ways to look at it and practice with it.
That's my plan.
I didn't really leave time for discussion tonight because I wanted to lay out a lot of words.
Before we ring out, let's just sit for a moment and breathe into the feeling in the body.
As we become more sensitive to feelings in the body, we can feel that everything we do has an imprint in the body, has an effect.
So just sitting here listening to my talk, and whatever happened today, the body is tuned into that.
See if we can stop from time to time and feel the body, feel the sensations, and let whatever it is just settle a little bit.
